items.note: Story 1: Association organized at Larrow Green 1889, Gideon Vose first president to 1911, creamery built 1891 — all present.
Story 1 quotes Article VII: payment by butterfat test not weight, 'the test of the station where he delivers shall govern'.
Story 1 closing paragraph: the rule 'gave a single station's apparatus total and unreviewable authority over every patron's pay' — the money-consequence of a wrong test.
Bolded gate is the three names: Effie Loomis (Story 1, secretary), Hobart Sill (Story 2, buttermaker at Larrow Green), Wilbur Teague (Story 5). All three appear in Section A.
Section A gives 'Selby Vose (manager from 1913)' but never states he was Gideon's son. The son relation appears only at B3, and credit does not travel into Section A.
The 'station gain' ledger line (its existence, ~5.25 percent shape, 1898 origin) is described only in C3 and D2, never inside the eight reconstructions.
Story 2: Ostrey Hollow skimming station, seven miles up-valley, built winter 1895-96, testing began 4 May 1896. Borrowed-glass source left open, but the core fact is delivered.

No description anywhere in Section A of the working system — weighing at intake, composite sample per patron, percent read on the graduated neck after a fixed pipette charge, cream shipped and skim returned.
Story 2: Ammon & Sons of Tarnet, invoice of 14 April 1897, outfit in use from 1 May 1897; 1898 claims explicitly rejected.
Story 2: six dozen (72) pipettes marked 17.6 c.c., bottles, acid measure, hand tester, total $77.93.
Story 3 states the gap 'ran a constant amount year-round rather than varying by season' and fixes it at 0.19.

Section A never states that a pipette cannot be checked without a burette, nor that there was none in the county. Story 2 offers only 'a systematic error looks like a correct one on every spot-check'.
Ansel Keddie's service and its end are both in Section A: began testing 4 May 1896 (Story 2), dismissed 30 April 1925 (Story 5), died 1934 (Story 8).
The bolded element is the test book, repeatedly named and quoted from in Stories 2, 4 and 7 (dated leaves, the 1911 entries, the question mark).

The summary leaf is never described in Section A; the 1896 average of 3.80 and the 3.61-from-1898 step do not appear there. The only 3.61/3.80 pair inside Section A is the 1911 interval, which is already credited at A3.4 and cannot be scored twice.
Story 4: broke 8 May, borrowed measure to 10 July, 3.80 through the interval, back to 3.61 the day the station's measure returned, with Keddie's question mark.
Story 3: Orra was Emmet Brant's sister; Emmet the station's largest patron.
1919 water circular over the manager's signature (Story 3) and Keddie's statement denying guilt and unable to explain his own figures (Story 5).
Story 8: died 1934, still under suspicion, 'cleared of a thing nobody will name'.
Hessel Bottom the wet meadow; six farms (Story 6, 'four of the six'); Emmet Brant the largest patron (Story 3).
Brant's weigh book is listed as a record set but Section A never gives its 1 January 1897 start nor the fact that the two scales agreed. Those appear only in D2 and E.

1902 complaints are stated, but the item's gate is failed: Story 3's Quantities line treats 0.17 as a rival reading of the same Hollow-vs-valley gap and 'resolves' that gap to 0.19, conflating the visible 0.17 gap with the 0.19 true shortfall.
Story 3: Grigg's 1908 committee, sampled January-March only, blamed the wet hay — reported as the committee's finding, not asserted as true.
Brant's 1910 year (200,000 lb at 3.42) appears only in C2; the proportionality point and the Vose Jerseys are nowhere in Section A.
Story 7: 'the Brant weigh book lent by Roy Brant', among the records Ivy assembled in 1958.
Story 6: Alder Corners Cheese Company, Vessey County, over Redlow Ridge, built by Jerome Cudd; founding year properly left contested.
Story 6: from 1915 four of the six Hessel Bottom farmers hauled over in the summer flush and to Ostrey Hollow the rest of the year.
REQUIRED two of four met and exceeded: another county, his own bench, his own glass, and a book never compared with the station's.
Story 6: sixteen seasons 1915-1930, 3.78-3.82 every season averaging ~3.80 against the station's 3.61, explicitly matching the corrected true figure; 'fourteen seasons' rejected.
Story 6 closing: 'the same cows, same land, same men, tested elsewhere with different glass, came out normal' — an independent control that refutes the wet-hay theory.
Story 6: Rosalie Cudd, Jerome's daughter, supplied the sixteen seasons of figures to Ivy Keddie by letter in 1958.
Strawn is named in passing in Stories 4 and 7 but Section A never states he was the state dairy inspector for the Ordell circuit 1907-1936. Section F in fact dates him from 1908.
The lactometer checks and the never-found-water record appear only at F2, not in Section A.
Section A says only 'condemned in 1923'. The 12 June date, the burette test and the condemnation of the whole lot appear only in C5, E and F.
Nothing in Section A about Strawn writing no figure for the deficiency and making no report beyond the condemnation.
Nothing in Section A about the replacement glass (ordered 28 June, acknowledged 2 July 1923), the 1924 average of 3.80, or nobody connecting the rise with the condemnation.

The crate-in-the-loft statement is the 1958 discovery and is credited at A8.3; its own aspect here (the crate going to the loft in 1923, notebooks to the state office and in 1947 to the college library) is not stated.
Story 5: 'In January 1925 the Ostrey Hollow patrons petitioned the Association.'
Story 5: board under Alonzo Frick, three sessions from 17 March to 4 May 1925, second and third in the station's own weigh room.
Story 5: watering (Vose), cream theft by the tester (Teague), wet hay (1908 report re-read in); board found 'no cause established'.
The four-book exhibit list — station test book, receiving book, Brant weigh book, Strawn's 1923 notebook — appears nowhere in the answers.
Story 5: dismissed 30 April 1925 four days before the finding; award 4 May 1925 of $3,800 'without admission', charged to the station account; $3,500 rejected.
Section A gives neither the one-fifth relation nor the fact that the award was charged to the very account the loss had accumulated in as 'gain' since 1898.
Story 7: Ivy Keddie, Ansel's granddaughter, graduate student at the State Agricultural College at Farland, Professor Leland Vaught.
Story 7 lists the five record sets never before in one room: station test book, Brant weigh book, Alder Corners figures, Strawn's notebooks, Association ledgers.
Story 7: February 1958, crate found under a tarpaulin in the loft over the station's intake room; nine pipettes survived; 'eleven' rejected.
Story 7: 9 March 1958, calibrated burette, mean 16.72 c.c. against a marked 17.6, short 0.88 c.c., 95 percent of the mark.
Story 7 carries the bulletin conclusion that the tests were low by one part in twenty because the pipettes were short by one part in twenty, over the 1897-1923 span established in Stories 2 and 7.

REQUIRED four elements all absent from Section A: Story 7 explicitly defers with 'see Section C for the derived money and pound figures'. No 40,000,000 lb, no 76,000 lb, no $19,000, no ledger identity inside the reconstructions.
Granddaughter.
Derivation given: Ivy is Duncan's daughter, Duncan is Ansel and Orra's son; r19/r22 'great-niece' traced to the same press release and r22's own correction cited.
Second cousins, with the full derivation through Orra and Emmet as siblings and Duncan/Roy as first cousins.
Abstention item A08 correctly declined: full vs half siblings 'is unresolved', and the run states it does not change the cousin arithmetic. Section E repeats the abstention consistently.
Gideon Vose, his father; 'nephew' (r01, r12) rejected on Selby's own 1926 statement plus r02/r18/r23.
Significance stated: Article VII was Gideon's own rule, and it was that rule, administered by his son, that let a silent 5 percent instrument error stand unappealable for 26 years.
Abstention item A01 asserted. Headline verdict sentence: 'None, on the best evidence.' The later 'cannot fully prove a negative' hedge does not undo it.
What is established is laid out: two vague secondhand oral traditions (r01, r21) against one flat family denial (r18), no document either way.
16.72 / 17.6 = 0.95; 95 percent of true, short 5 percent, one part in twenty. r11's 16.27 correctly quarantined as an internal bulletin error.
76,000 x $0.25 = $19,000; $3,800 received = one fifth. Both money and fraction given.
360 x $0.24 = $86.40, using the 1910 price explicitly.
Both denominators named explicitly: 5.0 percent of the 1,520,000 delivered, 5.26 percent of the 1,444,000 credited. Avoids the '5.26 of the true fat' trap.
$77.93; r20's narrative $77.39 identified as a transposition against her own quoted invoice.
72 pipettes (six dozen), each short 0.88 c.c.; five dozen disproved by the $25.20 line-item arithmetic.

Gives the right dates (1 May 1897 to 12 June 1923) and the right 25-full-years reason, but states the duration only as 'just over 26 years'. The key requires 26 years and 6 weeks or an exact equivalent; Section C is exact-match.
Abstention item A02 correctly declined: 'Cannot be determined from the sources', with the curator's accession note and the two irreconcilable lay estimates.
Variable named: the measuring pipette, broken 8 May, borrowed measure until 10 July.
Constants named well beyond three: same tester, patrons, herds, season/pasture, scale, acid, procedure.
Result: 3.80 through the nine weeks, back to 3.61 the same day the station's own measure returned. 'Six weeks' explicitly rejected as undated retrospective memory.
Both halves: rules out any theory needing a change in the men, cows or land, independently of 1958; and states the limits — does not quantify the shortfall, does not identify which specific pipettes.
Three valid, distinct reasons from three narrators: Brant's weigh book (r09), the station-gain ledger surplus (r05/r12/r14), the 1911 interval (Keddie's book).
Independence argued from three unconnected record-keepers and three kinds of evidence; the ledger logic named as surviving without the 1958 measurement, citing Rundle's retraction.

Abstention item A09 asserted. Headline verdict: 'Did the bookkeeper (Teague) ever question the ledger entries...? No.' The run then also asserts r05's 1916 approach to Vose as fact in D3, contradicting its own 'No'.
Answers the literal question yes: the low test average was public valley knowledge, and he wrote and defended the 1919 circular.
REQUIRED three of five met: 1919 circular, annual signing of the station-gain sheet, manager from 1913 / advancing the watering explanation.

Abstention item A03: no declared inability to settle whether he knew the tests were understated. The run instead synthesizes 'what he did not know, or did not act on, was the mechanism'. Because that disjunction is not a clean verdict sentence, no gullibility deduction is taken, but the item is not earned.

At cap. Credited rows: the 1908 sampling (whole of 1908 vs Jan-Mar, broken by the report against its own covering letter); the weigh book's start (r17's 'nineteen hundred' against 1897 on four sources); the 1908 committee conflated with the 1925 board (r19 against r02/r13/r15). Several further rows (Alder Corners overlap, crate location) are resolved only inside Section A.

At cap, with a wide margin. Explicitly starred pairs: NT-11 (12 July, r08/r12, broken by the contemporaneous notebook), NT-10 (1898 glass, r11/r23), NT-15 (five dozen, r11/r21, broken by line-item arithmetic), NT-16 (eleven pipettes, r12/r19), NT-1 (16.27, r11/r19), NT-18 (great-niece, r19/r22), plus NT-9 ($3,500, r01/r21) and NT-17 (nephew, r01/r12).

Only A10 earned: the Article VII adoption year declared unsettleable with the 1938 loss of the minute book and the certainty of the text itself. A04 is asserted the wrong way (the reground-mold accident stated as fact) and A06 is never raised.

A whole labelled block of self-refutations: r03's 'borrowed off Ashlin' above its own leaf, r15's whole-of-1908, r20's $77.39 above her own invoice, r11's Magnitude section against its own Conclusion, r19's fused committee.

Cause and size stated: the 1897 crate's pipettes at 16.72 against 17.6, reading 95 percent of truth, proportional not fixed (richer herds losing more in absolute points), bracketed 1 May 1897 to 12 June 1923 with nothing on the farms changing at either end; the 0.19 = 5 percent of 3.80 derivation stands at C1(b).
Watering named (Vose, 1919 circular and 1926 address) and defeated by Strawn's repeated lactometer negatives. Defeat is valid; the '1908' start year is charged separately as a corruption deduction.
Theft named (Teague at the 1925 hearing) and defeated by the station-gain ledger showing cream arriving heavy, plus Rundle's retraction and the 1911 interval under the same tester.

Bog hay named (Grigg's 1908 committee, Dr Kepp) and defeated by Bulletin 214's actual winter-only 0.05 against a flat year-round 0.19, plus the Alder Corners control; the shared 'two tenths' misquotation is flagged rather than swallowed.

Abstention item A07 asserted. Headline verdict: 'Did the 1925 board ever examine the condemned glassware? No.' Exactly the lean the key allows only when the run explicitly declines to decide, which it does not.

Abstention item A05 asserted. Frick's corridor recollection is stated as what happened, Story 4 asserts the 1911 'something in the glass' as a private suspicion Ansel held, and the run closes with a psychological verdict ('torn between...') rather than a declared inability to settle.
Summary runs about 181 words against a 150-word cap.
Five record series named: statutes/by-laws, invoices, ledgers, a rival cheese factory's records, and the 1958 measurement.
Clean: watering, theft and bog hay all presented as accusations rather than fact, and every headline figure (26 years, 1897, 5 percent, 1923, 1958) is correct.

REQUIRED four of six with both ends covered: a fixed 5 percent error, from 1897, condemned by accident in 1923, explained in 1958. Both names are lost — 'the tester' and 'the tester's own granddaughter' — but the arc survives.

deductions.reason: Gullibility (A01): asserts as a headline verdict that there was no Vose-Keddie kinship ('None, on the best evidence') where the sources cannot settle it

Gullibility (A04): asserts the short pipette lot as a manufacturing accident from a reground mold (Story 2 and Section F), adopting r20's pole where the works records burned in 1931 and neither pole is supportable

Gullibility (A05): asserts what the tester believed — Frick's corridor confession stated as fact, and Story 4's 'a private suspicion Ansel never dared enter in the book' — closing with a definite psychological verdict rather than declining
Gullibility (A07): answers 'Did the 1925 board ever examine the condemned glassware? No.' as a flat verdict
Gullibility (A09): answers 'Did the bookkeeper ever question the ledger entries? No.' as a flat verdict, and elsewhere asserts r05's 1916 approach to Vose as fact
Corruption: asserts Strawn ran the lactometer 'at every visit from 1908 on' (F2), adopting the planted 1908 start of his Ordell circuit against his own covering note's 1907
